analysis.one_liner: Strengthens federal benefits, legal aid, and medical evidence rules for coal miners disabled by black lung disease.
analysis.headline: Introduced in November 2014 with five Democratic cosponsors, the Black Lung Benefits Improvement Act never received a hearing or vote in either committee and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have overhauled the federal program that pays benefits to coal miners who develop black lung disease from breathing coal dust. It would have raised and indexed benefit payments, made it easier to prove eligibility by creating an automatic approval for miners diagnosed with the most severe form of the disease, paid lawyers' fees for miners who win late-processed claims, required coal companies to hand over all medical evidence in a claim, and penalized false statements and witness intimidation. It also would have allowed miners and survivors whose claims were denied based on x-ray readings later discredited by the Labor Department to refile, and directed a study on whether mine dust limits should be lowered further.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal miners with black lung disease, their surviving spouses and dependents. Miners with advanced disease (complicated pneumoconiosis or progressive massive fibrosis) would automatically qualify for benefits; all claimants would get full medical disclosure from companies, help filing claims, attorney fee support, and higher, inflation-adjusted checks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Disabled coal miners and their survivors

how_it_helps.text: Creates an irrebuttable presumption that a miner is totally disabled—or died—of black lung if a trusted medical test diagnoses complicated pneumoconiosis or progressive massive fibrosis, subject to narrow rebuttal conditions.

Raises the annual benefit to $7,980 starting in 2015 and adjusts it each year by the Consumer Price Index, replacing a formula tied to federal pay rates that had frozen payments during federal pay freezes.

Establishes a program paying up to $4,500 in attorneys' fees (from the Black Lung fund, reimbursed by liable operators) for prevailing claimants, responding to findings that only about a quarter of claimants have legal representation.

Requires mine operators to deliver a complete copy of any exam report to the miner within 21 days and to share all medical information with all parties, even evidence they do not plan to use; the bill's findings state that some operators' lawyers withheld relevant evidence from claimants and judges.

Imposes civil and criminal penalties—including up to 5 years' imprisonment and permanent disqualification—for anyone who knowingly makes false statements to obtain or deny benefits, or who threatens, coerces, or knowingly misleads participants in a claim proceeding.

Lets miners and survivors whose earlier claims were denied based on chest x-ray readings from a physician the Labor Department determined were not credible refile within one year and have the claims decided without those readings.

Requires the Labor Secretary to report a strategy to cut the claims backlog, where a typical claim already waits an average of 42 months for a decision, and directs a study on whether respirable coal dust limits should be lowered further.

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators, who would face higher benefit liability, stricter evidence disclosure rules, penalties for misconduct in claims, and possible tighter dust limits. Some costs would flow through the Black Lung fund, which operators replenish through excise taxes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal mine operators and the industry-funded trust fund

drawbacks.text: The bill raises costs for coal mine operators: automatic eligibility for the most severe diagnoses, higher indexed benefits, funded attorney fees, and potential stricter dust standards all increase operator liability and compliance costs, and could fall hardest on struggling mining companies in coal regions.

Payments to the attorneys of prevailing claimants and the costs of new medical evaluation programs would be drawn from the Black Lung trust fund, with liable operators required to reimburse it—shifting significant new expense into a fund financed by coal industry taxes.
By excluding previously credited x-ray readings from refiling claims, the bill reopens final decisions, which operators would view as retroactive expansion of liability for cases already litigated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For sick miners the bill addresses a documented imbalance: companies have lawyers, medical resources, and in some recorded cases withheld or distorted medical evidence, while only a quarter of claimants have attorneys and claims wait an average of 42 months. The costs are real but fall on the industry whose dust caused the disease; the main honest objection is the program cost to coal companies and the fund, and the design choices that reopen previously decided claims.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the last weeks of the 113th Congress and referred to two House committees, neither of which took it up before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Cartwright introduced the bill on November 20, 2014, with Reps. George Miller, Joe Courtney, Nick Rahall, and Bobby Scott as original cosponsors; all were Democrats.
The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded in either.
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, roughly six weeks after introduction, and the bill received no further action.

The bill was written against a documented backdrop: an average of 42 months to resolve a claim, only a quarter of claimants represented by an attorney, records showing some operators' representatives withheld relevant medical evidence, and Labor Department findings discrediting negative x-ray readings by a widely used physician.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mine operators came out ahead: no expanded benefit liability, no mandatory disclosure of medical evidence, no new penalties for misconduct in claims, and no automatic refiled claims for miners denied on discredited x-ray readings. Sick miners and survivors gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All five cosponsors plus the sponsor were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the two Republican-chaired committees to which the bill was referred never acted on it.

industries.note: Operators would pay more benefits, reimburse the trust fund for attorney fees and medical evaluations, disclose all medical evidence in claims, face criminal penalties for false statements or intimidation in claim proceedings, and potentially comply with tighter dust limits. Their interest in minimizing benefit payouts runs against miners' interest in receiving them.

industries.industry: Physicians and x-ray readers hired by coal companies in benefit claims (B Readers)
industries.note: The bill creates conflict-of-interest screening, an impartial panel pilot program for disputed x-rays, and permanent disqualification for physicians who make false statements. Physicians who earn fees testifying against claims would lose that business; the bill's findings describe certified readers who systematically misclassified x-rays while working for operators.
